text: Compare how Hardy in 'Neutral Tones' and Jennings in 'One Flesh' present relationships that have lost their emotional connection. You should consider the poets' use of language, form and structure, as well as the contexts in which the poems were written. [20 marks]
marks:
AO2 (15 marks):
Top band (13-15) Perceptive, sustained comparison. Hardy: pathetic fallacy (white sun, greyish leaves) drains the landscape; cyclical structure traps the speaker in the moment; 'tedious riddles' simile shows the lover's boredom. Jennings: paradox ('strangely apart, yet strangely close') captures marriage's complexity; 'flotsam from a former passion' suggests wreckage; regular stanzas mirror domestic routine. Both convey loss through environment/imagery, but Hardy's is bitter and Jennings's is contemplative.

Lower-mid band (4-6) Limited.

Keats: beauty is supernatural ('faery's child'), dangerous and destructive; ballad form creates a folk-tale of enchantment; cyclical structure traps the knight; beauty leads to 'palely loitering.' Byron: beauty is harmonious ('like the night / Of cloudless climes'), admired from a distance; regular ABABAB rhyme mirrors perfect balance; beauty is both external and moral ('A mind at peace'). Key contrast: Keats's beauty consumes; Byron's beauty is observed.

title: Form, Structure & Language
text: Compare how Barrett Browning in 'Sonnet 43' and Cooper Clarke in 'i wanna be yours' use the form of their poems to convey feelings of love. You should consider the poets' use of language, form and structure, as well as the contexts in which the poems were written. [20 marks]
marks:
AO2 (15 marks):
Top band (13-15) Perceptive comparison. Barrett Browning: Petrarchan sonnet — the most traditional love form — used by a woman, subverting the male tradition; tight rhyme scheme contains explosive emotion; anaphora of 'I love thee' builds within the sonnet's constraint. Cooper Clarke: no punctuation, no capitalisation, anaphora of 'I wanna be your' — deliberately anti-literary; performance poem meant to be heard; domestic imagery replaces roses and stars. Key comparison: both use anaphora to build devotion, but through radically different registers and forms.
Upper-mid band (10-12) Clear comparison.
Mid band (7-9) Some comparison.
Lower-mid band (4-6) Limited.
Lower band (1-3) Simple.

Top band (5) Barrett Browning's Victorian context (elopement, defying her father) vs Cooper Clarke's punk movement (working-class Salford, rejecting literary elitism). Both revolutionary in their contexts.
Upper-mid band (4) Clear.
Mid band (3) Some.
Lower-mid band (2) Limited.
Lower band (1) Simple.

marks:

Duffy: free verse with irregular stanzas — rejecting formal convention mirrors her rejection of romantic cliches; short imperative lines ('Take it') become increasingly commanding; the poem darkens structurally from gift to threat. Both use structure to reveal attitudes: the Duke's control, Duffy's escalating intensity.

text: Compare how Keats in 'La Belle Dame Sans Merci' and Armitage in 'The Manhunt' use form to convey the experience of being trapped by love. You should consider the poets' use of language, form and structure, as well as the contexts in which the poems were written. [20 marks]
marks:
AO2 (15 marks):
Top band (13-15) Perceptive comparison. Keats: ballad form — cyclical structure traps the knight on the cold hillside; shortened fourth lines create incompleteness; the refrain-like return mirrors the repeating pattern of enchantment and loss. Armitage: couplets that move ever inward — the structure itself is a journey from which there is no easy return; 'Only then would he let me' controls the pace; the poem ends before resolution. Both poets use form to enact entrapment, but Keats's is mythic and Armitage's is psychological.

title: Social Conflict & Identity

The two-stanza structure mirrors two stages: physical separation at birth and emotional separation as the child grows. 'First fierce confrontation' uses alliteration to stress intensity. The present-tense 'Still I am fighting / You off' shows the conflict is ongoing — motherhood is a perpetual negotiation between holding on and letting go.

The oxymoronic quality captures the poem's core truth: the mother-child relationship is simultaneously loving and combative.
